o: Split nums into exactly k contiguous pieces minimizing the maximum piece-XOR. With n ≤ 250, an O(k·n²) min-max DP is easily fast enough: dp[j][i] = best answer for the first i elements split into j parts, transitioning over the last cut point using prefix XORs for O(1) piece-XOR queries. A slicker alternative binary-searches the answer and greedily checks feasibility.
k: Prefix XOR gives any subarray's XOR in O(1): xor(i..j) = pre[j+1] ^ pre[i].
Min-max partition is a classic DP: minimize over cut points of the max(left answer, last piece XOR).
The feasibility predicate 'can split into ≤ k pieces each with XOR ≤ m' is greedily checkable, enabling binary search on m.

a.i: dp[j][i] is the minimum possible maximum XOR splitting the first i elements into j parts. The last part is nums[p..i-1] with XOR pre[i]^pre[p]; combine with dp[j-1][p] via max and take the minimum over p. Only states with j ≤ i are meaningful.
s: For j = 1..k, i = j..n: dp[j][i] = min over p in [j-1, i) of max(dp[j-1][p], pre[i]^pre[p]).
a.t: O(k·n²) — about 15.6M operations at the limits (n = k = 250)

a.n: Approach 2: Binary search on the answer + greedy check
a.i: The predicate 'the array can be split into at most k contiguous pieces, each with XOR ≤ m' is monotone in m. Greedy check: extend the current piece while its XOR stays ≤ m; when adding an element would exceed m, cut before it. Taking maximal pieces minimizes the piece count, so the greedy uses the fewest possible pieces. Binary search the smallest feasible m over [0, 2³⁰).
s: Define ok(m): scan left to right, cur = 0; if cur^x > m, start a new piece with cur = x (fail if a single x > m).
Binary search the minimum m with ok(m) true.
a.t: O(n log V) — 30 greedy scans of the array

w: Prefer the DP in an interview for its obvious correctness; offer binary search as the optimization follow-up (it scales to huge n). Pitfall: XOR is not monotone under extension, so the greedy must cut exactly when the running XOR would exceed m — cutting earlier never helps. Watch the exact-k vs at-most-k distinction: padding with singleton pieces shows at-most-k suffices when n ≥ k.
